The stew was dark and rich, eel and something rooty, and Alaric ate it standing by the stove while Salta rewrapped Hemm's binding and Hemm talked at the ceiling about sluice gates. The third bowl stayed on the hearth-edge for whoever wanted it.

The road to Marsh Hollow ran off the dam spine through cut peat and reed beds, the sky going from copper to grey behind the western treeline. Frogs started up in the ditches as the light failed. Twice something small broke cover ahead of him and once a heron lifted off a channel with a clap of wings, and each time the sound was behind him before he'd finished turning his head. A peat-cutter passed him going the other way with a barrow and a lit spill of rushlight, and gave him a nod and nothing else.

Marsh Hollow announced itself by smell first — woodsmoke and fish oil and the sour sweetness of the tanners' yards — then by lamplight strung along a low street that followed the water. The village was small, a single street of stone-footed houses with a market square at its heart, mostly shut up for the evening. The Guild hall sat on the square's far side, a long building of dark timber with a lamp burning over its door and the Guild's mark cut into the lintel.

Inside, the front room was one open space — a hearth, a notice board, a counter of scarred oak running the width of the room. The counter lamp was lit but turned down low. Behind it stood a grey-haired clerk with a ledger open and a candle burned down to within a thumb of the stick, closing up for the night. She looked over at the sound of the door.

"Counter's shutting," she said. "If it can wait till morning, it waits. If it can't, say so quick."

The coin clicked into his pouch — eight copper and the silver, heavy and real. Marda took a knife from the desk drawer, cut a heel of bread and a wedge of cheese off the shelf without getting up, and wrapped them in a square of cloth.

"There. Mind you eat it today; it's not getting younger." She pushed the parcel across and watched him take it. "And you're welcome for the lot. First work I've had done in that warehouse in three days of asking."

At his question she sat back and squinted at him, the pen resting against her lip.

"The Guild hall. You're one of those, are you — the red eyes should have told me sooner." She waved the pen vaguely northward. "Out of the yard, left on Tanner's Row, follow it to the end and you'll hit the Weavers' Walk. Cross that, past the dye houses — you'll smell them before you see them — and the Guild hall sits on the little square beyond, white stone, big doors, a board out front you can't miss. Ten minutes' walk if you don't dawdle."

She went back to her ledger, then looked up once more.

"They post work on that board every morning. If you're after more of this kind of thing—" a nod toward the warehouse doors, "—get there early. The good slips go quick."

The yard beyond the office was bright and ordinary again, the cart man from earlier gone, a boy shoveling coal into a barrow by the gates. Tanner's Row ran left from the doors, cobbles still damp from the morning, busy with the day's noise — cartwheels, a hammer somewhere, gulls over the rooftops.

deltas.why: payment for the warehouse rat work
deltas.said: The coin clicked into his pouch — eight copper and the silver, heavy and real.

deltas.where: Out of the yard, left on Tanner's Row to the end, cross Weavers' Walk past the dye houses; white stone on the little square beyond, ten minutes' walk

deltas.text: Marda paid Alaric for clearing the rats and gave him bread and cheese; she told him the Guild hall lies past Weavers' Walk and that good slips on the board go quick in the morning.
